guide.summary: Modern physics covers phenomena classical physics can't explain: light as photons (photoelectric effect), quantized atomic energy levels and spectra, the wave nature of matter (de Broglie), mass-energy equivalence, and nuclear decay, half-life, fission, and fusion.

sections.heading: Photons and the photoelectric effect
sections.body: Light comes in quanta (photons) with energy E = hf = hc/λ (hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm). In the photoelectric effect, light ejects electrons from a metal only if each photon's energy exceeds the work function φ: K_max = hf − φ. Below the threshold frequency f₀ = φ/h, no electrons are emitted regardless of intensity. Increasing intensity increases the number of photoelectrons (current) but not their maximum kinetic energy; increasing frequency increases K_max. The stopping potential satisfies eV_stop = K_max. A graph of K_max (or V_stop) vs. f is linear with slope h (or h/e) and horizontal intercept f₀.

sections.heading: Atomic energy levels and spectra
sections.body: Electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels (negative values relative to ionization at 0). When an electron drops from a higher to a lower level, it emits a photon with energy equal to the difference: hf = E_high − E_low; absorption requires a photon of exactly that energy. Each element has a unique line spectrum. Larger energy gaps correspond to higher-frequency, shorter-wavelength photons. The number of possible emission lines from level n down to the ground state is n(n − 1)/2.

sections.heading: Wave-particle duality
sections.body: Particles have a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p = h/(mv). Electron diffraction confirms matter waves. Heavier or faster particles have shorter wavelengths, which is why wave effects are noticeable only for tiny particles. Light shows both wave behavior (interference) and particle behavior (photoelectric effect).

sections.heading: Nuclear physics
sections.body: Mass-energy equivalence: E = mc² (1 u ≈ 931 MeV). The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of its nucleons; this mass defect corresponds to binding energy. Fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion combines light nuclei; both release energy because products have greater binding energy per nucleon. Decays conserve charge and nucleon number: alpha decay emits ⁴₂He (A − 4, Z − 2); beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton, emitting an electron and antineutrino (Z + 1); beta-plus emits a positron (Z − 1); gamma decay emits a high-energy photon with no change in A or Z. Radioactive decay is random; after n half-lives, (½)ⁿ of the original nuclei remain.

keyTakeaways: K_max = hf − φ; intensity changes number, not energy.
Photon energy = difference between atomic levels.
Decays conserve charge and nucleon number.
commonMistakes: Claiming brighter light below threshold ejects electrons.
Using wavelength in meters with hc in eV·nm.
Treating energy levels as positive values.
Forgetting that beta-minus decay increases the atomic number.
Thinking a single nucleus decays at a predictable time.
examTips: Photoelectric graphs: slope = h (or h/e), intercept = threshold frequency.
Energy-level diagrams: compute differences, then convert to λ.
Balance nuclear equations by checking top (A) and bottom (Z) numbers.
Lab FRQs may graph stopping voltage vs. frequency.
guide.cramSheet:
**Photon:** E = hf = hc/λ · 1240 eV·nm

**Photoelectric:** K_max = hf − φ · eV_stop = K_max · f₀ = φ/h · intensity → number

**Atoms:** hf = E_high − E_low · line spectra

**Matter waves:** λ = h/mv

**Nuclear:** E = mc² · 1 u = 931 MeV · α (−4, −2) · β⁻ (0, +1) · β⁺ (0, −1) · γ (0, 0)

**Half-life:** (½)ⁿ

vocab.definition: A quantum of electromagnetic energy with E = hf.
The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a metal surface.
The minimum frequency of light that can eject electrons from a given metal.
The potential difference needed to stop the most energetic photoelectrons: eV = K_max.
A discrete allowed energy for an electron in an atom.
The set of specific wavelengths emitted by an element's atoms.
The wavelength associated with a moving particle: λ = h/p.
The difference between the mass of separated nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.
The energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons.
Emission of a helium-4 nucleus, reducing A by 4 and Z by 2.
A neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino; Z increases by 1.
The time for half of a radioactive sample's nuclei to decay.

distractors.A: Counts only direct transitions to lower adjacent levels.

practice.stem: A proton and an electron have the same de Broglie wavelength. Which is true?

choices.text: They have the same momentum, so the electron moves much faster.
They have the same kinetic energy.

practice.explanation: λ = h/p; equal λ means equal p. The lighter electron needs a higher speed (and has more kinetic energy).

practice.stem: Light of fixed frequency above threshold shines on a metal. The intensity is doubled. Which graph change is correct?

choices.text: The stopping potential doubles; the current is unchanged.
The photocurrent doubles; the stopping potential is unchanged.

practice.explanation: More photons eject more electrons, each with the same maximum energy.

practice.stem: Why does fusion of light nuclei (like hydrogen into helium) release energy?

choices.text: The product has more mass than the reactants.
The product nucleus has greater binding energy per nucleon, so total mass decreases and the difference is released as energy.

practice.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon increases from hydrogen up to iron.

practice.prompt:
Students shine light of several frequencies on a metal plate in a vacuum tube and measure the stopping potential for each frequency.

| Frequency (× 10¹⁴ Hz) | 6.0 | 7.0 | 8.0 | 9.0 | 10.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stopping potential (V) | 0.18 | 0.60 | 1.01 | 1.43 | 1.84 |

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe how the students could vary the frequency of light and measure the stopping potential, including one way to reduce uncertainty.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Describe a graph of stopping potential vs. frequency, including axis labels and a best-fit line.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Use your graph to determine a value for Planck's constant. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Use your graph to determine the work function of the metal, in eV.

rubric.description: Use filters, LEDs, or a monochromator to select frequencies; increase reverse voltage until the photocurrent just reaches zero and record that voltage.
Repeat measurements and average; use many frequencies; shield from stray light.
Stopping potential (V) vs. frequency (Hz) with labels, units, linear scales.
eV_stop = hf − φ, so slope = h/e.
Extend line: V-intercept ≈ −2.3 V (or threshold f₀ ≈ 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz).

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Use a set of LEDs or color filters to produce light of known frequencies. For each frequency, apply a reverse voltage between the plate and the collector and increase it until the photocurrent measured by a sensitive ammeter just drops to zero; that voltage is the stopping potential. Repeat each measurement several times and average, and cover the apparatus to block stray light.

B. Plot stopping potential (V) on the vertical axis and frequency (× 10¹⁴ Hz) on the horizontal axis with linear scales. The points lie on a straight line; draw a best-fit line through them.

C. Slope ≈ (1.84 V − 0.18 V)/(10.0 − 6.0) × 10¹⁴ Hz = 1.66/(4.0 × 10¹⁴) ≈ 4.15 × 10⁻¹⁵ V·s. From eV_stop = hf − φ, V_stop = (h/e)f − φ/e, so slope = h/e. h = (4.15 × 10⁻¹⁵)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

D. Extending the line to f = 0 gives a vertical intercept of about −2.3 V, so φ/e ≈ 2.3 V and the work function is about 2.3 eV. (Equivalently, the threshold frequency is about 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz, and φ = hf₀ ≈ 2.3 eV.)
